title: I started making an age-of-sail game the day Fable 5.2 launched. Here's what I have so far
author: Agreeable-Round-1405
selftext:
10 days later, Vaelen is online (it's a work in progress, don't shame me too hard pls). 



You start in a skiff and trade, fish and fight your way up to a man-o'-war. Single player, runs in a browser tab. I'd recommend setting the graphics to Medium and frame rate to Steady and then reloading the page (Ultra is a bit too demanding and not very visually different IMO)



[https://aj8uppal.github.io/vaelen/](https://aj8uppal.github.io/vaelen/)

WebGL2 on desktop, no mobile yet! But maybe soon



Fable wrote almost all the code through Claude Code, including the ocean, the sky, and the sails, which are actual simulated cloth. Nothing is hand modelled either: the ships, towns and islands come out of Blender scripts it wrote and runs headless. Crew are from Meshy, and sound and music are ElevenLabs.



What helped most was giving it ways to check its own work. There are scripts that drive headless Chrome, play the opening with real clicks, sail every region looking for errors, and time frames before and after a render change. I've also loved using Granola for my playtests, it really helps when you're making a game/app that you actually want to play/use - you can just playtest and call out things you like, want different, and then edit the transcript, pass to your agents, and hit the hay.



The main difficulty (I'm sure most here will agree) is making the core game loop polished, airtight, and novel. I've loved playing it so far but there's a few things that need work (you can hire a crewmember to instantly move from port to port, which means you can just fulfill oodles of missions and sort of bypass the whole sailing-to-grind mechanic). But iteration is key and as I mentioned earlier, actually playing the game helps a lot for coherently providing the nudges and direction that I want.



Tell me how it runs on your machine and where you got bored! Would love any and all feedback, I want to make the game mechanic more engaging. I have a local build with better UI, better onboarding, and improvements to graphics/gameplay that I'll push this weekend once I playtest some more.

comments.author: United_Ad5772
comments.body:
Good day. Greeting from sailor. It will be great to add WebGL1 support - usually it is no big adaptation.  
Which license you have in mind?

replies.author: Agreeable-Round-1405
replies.body:
Thanks! The ocean renderer uses WebGL2 features like texture arrays, so WebGL1 would take a separate rendering path rather than a quick toggle. What device or browser were you trying it on? I’m also looking into WebGPU (optionally) which would make a few things like the cloth / sails smoother. But WebGL2 has been remarkable thus far

I also haven’t settled on a license yet hehe

comments.author: niord
comments.body: My I ask how did you create the water and especially foam on water shader?

replies.author: Agreeable-Round-1405
replies.body:
It’s a custom WebGL2 shader. The ocean uses several layers of FFT waves, and the boats sample the same wave spectrum on the CPU. For the foam, I combine three masks: where the wave crests bunch up, where ships leave wakes, and where the water meets the shore. Then I sample a foam texture at two scales so thin foam breaks up into little lace patterns instead of looking like flat white paint.

I’ll work this weekend on making the water and some other components open source! I didn’t anticipate others would want to reuse some of the assets but I’m more than happy to share :)

comments.author: K_kkomi
comments.body:
The visuals are absolutely stunning, especially the ocean and simulated sails! It's incredible that you built this in just 10 days.

I've also been making an indie game with Claude Code, and I totally agree that getting the gameplay loop right is much harder than getting the code to work.

Did automated testing make a big difference in your development process?

replies.author: Agreeable-Round-1405
replies.body:
Automated testing is definitely huge for iteration, but of course can be expensive with tokens. But key for making sure I hadn’t broken anything while iterating

I used scripted runs with real keyboard inputs to replay the first voyage, visit all 12 harbors, and exercise things like boarding, sinking, and salvage. That helped me catch regressions, but it couldn’t tell me where a new player would get confused or bored. That’s the part I’m hoping to learn from this playtest.

Playtests really are key, nothing will beat the feedback you give by actually playing for an hour! (On that note, any and all feedback you have I would be extremely grateful!)

replies.author: K_kkomi
replies.body: That's a really good point. I've been using Claude Code for my own game, and automated tests have been incredibly helpful for catching bugs during development. But passing tests doesn't necessarily mean the game is fun or intuitive for a new player. I think getting feedback from people who have never played your game is especially valuable. Good luck with the playtest!

replies.author: Agreeable-Round-1405
replies.body:
100%. The part that’s nagging at all of us I’m sure is “if I can make this game with a few prompts, anyone can”. 

What really separates that *should* be simple: putting in effort and time, pouring your own ideas and taste into the game. Playing it myself, friends playing, you all playing! Absolutely invaluable feedback and I’m super excited to try out some new ideas and see where it goes. Really wasn’t expecting this many people to play and weigh in so soon, I am now really thinking about what a better platform (or platforms) could be for it, and will definitely open source the water and other parts of the environment that people like!

comments.author: SevenStepsEntertain
comments.body: How did you paint the ship sir? I understand claude can model in blender but did it also paint in blender?

replies.author: Agreeable-Round-1405
replies.body: Sort of! Fable wrote Blender scripts that built the ships and marked which parts were bare wood, painted bands, or trim. There wasn’t any hand-painting in Blender. The ships use wood textures from Poly Haven, and the game’s shader does the rest in the browser: it colors the paint bands, varies the finish plank by plank, and adds weathering and a wet band near the waterline.

replies.author: SevenStepsEntertain
replies.body: Cool! Also why did you choose headless? Is it better than MCP?

replies.author: Agreeable-Round-1405
replies.body:
Great question - I think both are good for different reasons

I went headless because the ships are generated from scripts. Fable could edit the Python, run Blender from the terminal, and rebuild all seven hulls without clicking around in the UI. The nice part is that if I change how the trim works, I can rebuild every ship the same way.

They solve different things: headless is how Blender runs, and MCP is one way to give the agent tools to talk to it. For Vaelen, the Python scripts and terminal were enough!

comments.author: bluesmaker
comments.body:
This is excellent from the short bit I played! Genuinely.  

I do have some feedback. 

Just my opinion: I don't like browser-based games. It's not 2006. I'm not in high school. I have my own computer. I play games off Steam. It's rare I do not use Steam. Maybe you are developing it as browser based for now but may change it over once it's come together more. 

The map: it looks uninspired to me. I see like 5 groups of islands, and they all have about the same number of islands, with similar shapes and sizes. I'd say, you should only repeat that 2 or 3 times. Make them more varied. Sea of Thieves has some nice island ideas you can look at for inspiration. 

The spyglass: I'm sure you know this is a problem, but when you use it, it zooms in from the same behind-the-ship perspective. It should zoom in from the character's perspective, or from the bow of the boat. 

Fishing: when trying to learn fishing, the screen and text moved too fast. Like you do G, then SPACE, then there's something you need to hold SPACE for and on that menu I don't have enough time to read. Maybe solve with a tutorial fishing thing where right around where you start you have a longer time to catch.... I finally figured it out, but it wasn't clear for a bit. I like the idea but this part could use some change. Like maybe the progress bar is replaced with a sound+graphic of some kind. Like a rod reeling in and/or fishing rod strain, etc. Something to make it more engaging.

The battle music should not be triggered just by using cannons. Maybe triggered by like 3 cannon shorts quickly, or by nearing a hostile ship, or once you fire on a ship...

The dolphins following the boat are super cool. But I hope they do not do that too much. Would take away the charm. It's a nice idea to have it happen right away. Something for a new player to marvel at. But when they did it again, like 5 minutes later, I began to wonder if they'd be around too much. They did react to my cannon and scatter, so that's a nice touch. 

I docked at Coral City to sell the one fish I got. The port screen UI is nice. Easy to parse. I think one thing to work towards would be more interesting scenes happening on the right side of the screen. Like "harbor" can show the view you have now, but "tavern" changes that view to a tavern scene, etc. Bonus points if each city's locations have their own unique look. Bonus bonus points if the time of day changes the scene. This kind of thing would make visiting town feel like more of a reprieve after sailing adventures.  

I like that you're thinking about how to polish the core gameplay loop. I didn't really play enough to develop an idea about how the various options of sailing goals. Are cannon balls unlimited? What about your own supplies (like wood and water). Maybe a mechanic about the "endurance" (the term meaning how long a ship can operate unreplenished while doing its job) would make the player need to make some meaningful decisions. 

Are there storms? Storms seem essential for a sailing game!

It run fine on my PC. I have a relatively strong gaming PC. 

Again, looks like the game is coming along very well!

replies.author: Agreeable-Round-1405
replies.body:
Wow… this is great feedback, thank you.

I’ve been thinking about iPad to reach a broader audience but Steam would be great too, I haven’t used Steam since Realm of the Mad God back in the day 😁

On the map point, I do agree. The world could use more nuance, at this point I fear it gets repetitive after a few journeys and once you upgrade to the best ship and have visited all the islands, there’s not much to do. I’ll definitely look at Sea of Thieves for some inspiration

Yeah the spyglass is a bit buggy, and downright useless at points 😂 fishing and probably more things need a big UI polish and better onboarding. In general many ai-dev games i see and even ones I’ve made have a visual fatigue problem so I need to find a nice clean way to present the information!

Battle music - I like the idea of the 3 cannons, and also yes the dolphins are perhaps too fond of the boat 😂 a few of those things that happen a bit rarely would add to the magic and intrigue, I agree

Also love the idea of using the right half of the harbor UI, it currently doesn’t do much and is just begging for something nice to be there. The dynamic scenes is an excellent idea

I’m glad it’s smooth, and there are storms! After a few minutes of sailing around you should encounter one :)

For the core game mechanic - yeah that’s the part I need to nail down, and always open to feedback and ideas. The generic cannonball is unlimited but you can get grapeshot and other kinds of projectiles by buying them at harbors. The endurance and limited resource thing is great too, I think leaning into realism here in a tasteful way is going to be a direction I seriously pursue

\-

Thanks again for playing, I’ll hope to get some of this feedback incorporated (and more) this weekend 🙌

comments.author: CroAtTheTop
comments.body:
May I ask, what approach did you take with the creation of the assets?

As that is my current biggest painpoint/blocker. Never able to create the assets the way I want them, endless loop of fixes and changes, with different approaches.

replies.author: Agreeable-Round-1405
replies.body:
My approach was ton split it up by asset type. Fable wrote Python scripts that run Blender headless to generate the ships and buildings. For the ships, Blender handled the shape and marked which parts were wood, paint, or trim. I used Poly Haven for the base textures and let the game shader handle the paint colors and weathering. The crew went through Meshy instead.

If I were starting again, I’d get one asset looking right in the actual game before making a whole set. Pick a reference, render the asset at the camera distance and lighting players will actually see, then give feedback on one thing at a time: silhouette first, materials second. Once that one looks right, use it as the reference for the rest. The nice part of scripting the ships was that if the trim looked wrong, I could fix it in one place and rebuild all seven hulls instead of touching each model by hand.
